text.p: Pressure increased on the Belgian government on Thursday as a liberal opposition party offered to trade places in the ruling coalition with the scandal-torn francophone socialists.

A bribes-for-contracts scandal widened as a former Belgian army colonel was charged with corruption and moves were reportedly underway for police to interview the former leader of the PS party of French-speaking socialists.
The offer by the PRL liberals to get a foothold in the centre-left coalition raised pressure on the current four partners to resolve the crisis without losing face.
"With the PRL in the government things would change quickly," Louis Michel, chairman of the francophone liberal party PRL told Belgian radio.

The Dutch-speaking Christian-democratic CVP, the largest coalition partner, said the request was premature. "I have never questioned this coalition. We are not at the stage of changing coalition partners," chairman Marc Van Peel told the radio.

A series of bribery scandals, notably involving the PS, has rocked Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene's government of Christian-democrats and socialists from both sides of the French-Dutch language divide.
Earlier this week Van Peel said his party's confidence in the PS had been "severely shocked" and he urged the party to get its house in order within days.
The cracks in the coalition have undermined the Belgian franc with foreign investors becoming nervous about the future of the government.

Stock and bond markets, however, shrugged off suggestions of a government collapse with traders firmly believing in renewed behind-the-scenes efforts by Dehaene to paper over the cracks so that he can safely finish his work on bringing Belgium into Europe's single currency union at the scheduled start in 1999.
An opinion poll published on Thursday showed nearly half Belgians believing the PS should leave the government, but less than a quarter expecting elections in the coming months.
The latest scandal centres on allegations that French aerospace group group Dassault paid millions of Belgian francs in kickbacks to politicians to win an air force order in 1989.

Last week two former senior PS officials were arrested and charged with corruption. Their lawyers have said they received 30 million francs (about $1 million) from Dassault on behalf of the PS but Dassault has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing.

The investigation has led to numerous calls from the opposition and coalition politicians for the PS to jettison those responsible for party finances in the late eighties, in particular the then chairman Guy Spitaels.

RTBF radio said on Thursday the Liege court overseeing the bribes probe had requested the lifting of the parliamentary immunity of Spitaels, who is now the president of the Walloon regional parliament, to be able to interview him.
A Liege court spokesman declined to comment.
Spitaels said in a statement he would cooperate fully with investigators, but reiterated he was totally "oblivious to the allegations made in the so-called Dassault affair."
"I will willingly make myself available and give my full agreement to help establish, as soon as possible, the whole truth in the dossier that motivates this demand," he said.
Another Liege court official said earlier on Thursday that a former Belgian army colonel had also been charged with corruption in the Dassault probe.
